appraisal_events.evidence: "Elles étaient pressées" as an excuse the narrator recognizes as insincere, followed by: "même les grands hommes sont, en certaines choses, pareils aux gens vulgaires, prennent les excuses journalières dans le même répertoire qu'eux, comme le pain quotidien chez le même boulanger."
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator exposes Elstir's evasive excuse as a stock, insincere phrase, explicitly generalizing that even great men fall back on the same banal excuses as vulgar people, locally undercutting Elstir's stature.

appraisal_events.evidence: "le coup d'œil du grand peintre la détruit en une seconde"; "Maintenant déchue, située hors de son propre type où elle trônait invulnérable, elle n'est plus qu'une femme quelconque en la supériorité de qui nous avons perdu toute foi."
appraisal_events.explanation: The extended meditation on Elstir's portrait shows his artistic genius dismantling the factitious 'harmony' Odette has imposed on her appearance, reducing her from an invulnerable, singular type to an ordinary woman whose superiority we no longer credit.

status_effects.explanation: Elstir's petty, formulaic excuse-making momentarily lowers him by revealing an ordinary, evasive side beneath his greatness.
The passage's dominant theoretical movement elevates Elstir's artistic authority, crediting his genius with the power to dissolve a sitter's cultivated self-image and impose his own truth.
Odette is locally diminished as Elstir's portrait strips away the constructed 'type' underlying her beauty and identity, leaving her an ordinary woman in whom the narrator's faith is lost.

ambiguities: The narrator's comment that 'even great men' resort to the same vulgar excuses is partly an indulgent generalization and partly a pointed diminishment of Elstir; how much irony versus straightforward exposure is intended is not fully resolved.
